extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and advanced undergraduates learning algebraic geometry (readers of Vakil's 'The Rising Sea')
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition and usable criteria for (1) when Čech cohomology agrees with derived-functor cohomology on schemes, and (2) definitions, examples, and practical criteria for flatness of modules, sheaves, and morphisms, with exercises and proof sketches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 23.5.1 — Čech vs derived-functor cohomology
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose X is a quasicompact separated scheme, and F is a quasicoherent sheaf. Then the Čech cohomology of F agrees with the derived functor cohomology of F.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statement should be made precise: the isomorphism is functorial in F and respects long exact sequences; there is an extension to higher pushforwards. Proof idea: choose a finite affine open cover and an injective resolution of F, form the associated double complex, and use the two filtrations of the spectral sequence to identify one orientation with derived-functor cohomology and the other with Čech cohomology. See also Leray-style generalization (Remark 23.5.6) and exercises 23.5.G/H for functoriality and compatibility with long exact sequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functoriality and long exact sequence compatibility for the Čech-derived isomorphism
rubrics_metrics.description: The isomorphism between Čech and derived-functor cohomology should be functorial in F and should respect connecting homomorphisms so that the long exact sequences match.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The spectral sequence argument is functorial in E0 (the double complex), which yields the required functoriality. Exercise 23.5.G asks to verify the commutativity of the square comparing Hi(X,F)→RiΓ(X,F) with the corresponding map for G under a morphism F→G. Exercise 23.5.H asks to show the isomorphisms induce isomorphisms of long exact sequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ingredient (A) — Injectives have no higher Čech cohomology
rubrics_metrics.description: If (X, OX) is a ringed space, Q is an injective OX-module, and X = ⋃i Ui is a finite open cover, then Q has no i-th Čech cohomology with respect to this cover for i > 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is justified because injective OX-modules are flasque (Exercise 23.4.H) and flasque sheaves have vanishing positive-degree Čech cohomology with respect to finite covers (Exercise 23.5.C). Use induction on the number of opens and the long exact sequence of Čech cohomology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ingredient (B) — Quasicoherent sheaves on affine schemes have vanishing higher derived functor cohomology
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is an affine scheme and F is a quasicoherent sheaf on X, then RiΓ(X,F) = 0 for i > 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proved by induction on i using an injective resolution and a tailored affine cover so that a chosen cocycle is locally a boundary; combine with the spectral-sequence double-complex argument (section 23.5.4). The quasicoherence hypothesis is used at the spot where vanishing of Čech cohomology on affines is invoked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise 23.5.A — Restriction of injectives is injective
rubrics_metrics.description: If Q is an injective OX-module and i: U ↪ X is the inclusion of an open subset, then Q|U is injective as an OU-module.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hint: use that i^{-1} has an exact left adjoint i_! (extension by zero). Diagrams in the text illustrate how extension by zero interacts with injectivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise 23.5.B — Right adjoints to exact functors preserve injectives
rubrics_metrics.description: If (F,G) is an adjoint pair of additive functors between abelian categories and F is exact, then G sends injectives to injectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the adjunction and exactness of F to check Ext-vanishing; the exercise is used to justify that restrictions of injectives remain injective in local arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectral-sequence double-complex proof strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: To compare Čech and derived-functor cohomology, take an injective resolution of F and a finite affine open cover, form the associated double complex (Čech degree vs injective resolution degree), and analyze the two filtrations yielding two spectral sequences whose E2 pages give derived functor cohomology and Čech cohomology respectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One filtration uses vanishing of Čech cohomology of injectives (A) to collapse to Qi(X) columns; the other uses vanishing of higher RiΓ on affines (B) to collapse all but row 0 giving the Čech complex. Convergence at E2 yields the desired identification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remark (Leray-type generalization)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a sheaf F on a topological space X has the property that RiΓ(U_{i1}∩...∩U_{ik}, F)=0 for all finite intersections of a cover {Ui}, then the cohomology of F on X can be computed by the Čech cohomology of that cover.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This shows one can compute cohomology by a single cover if cohomology vanishes on all finite intersections — no need to colimit over refinements. See Remark 23.5.6.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition (24.2.1) — Flat module
rubrics_metrics.description: An A-module M is flat if the functor M ⊗_A (–) : Mod_A → Mod_A is exact (equivalently, preserves exact sequences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recall tensoring is always right-exact; flatness is the additional left-exactness property. Use Tor characterization (Exercise 23.1.C): M is flat iff Tor^A_1(M,N)=0 for all N. Basic examples and consequences follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Key examples of flat modules
rubrics_metrics.description: Free A-modules (even infinite rank) and projective modules are flat. Localizations S^{-1}A (and modules obtained by localization) are flat over A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freeness/projectivity: direct-check via exactness. Localization is exact (Exercise 1.6.G(a)). These give easy tests and constructions of flat modules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observation 24.2.2 — Flat ⇒ torsion-free (detecting non-flatness)
rubrics_metrics.description: If x is a non-zerodivisor of A and M is a flat A-module, then multiplication by x on M is injective; in particular, flat modules are torsion-free over integral domains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the exact functor M ⊗_A (–) to 0 → A --×x→ A to deduce injectivity on M. This yields a simple way to show modules are not flat by finding torsion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 24.2.3 — Flatness is a stalk/prime-local property
rubrics_metrics.description: An A-module M is flat if and only if Mp is a flat A_p-module for all prime ideals p ⊂ A (equivalently, checking at primes or maximal ideals suffices).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses localization and exactness of tensor; if Mp is flat for all p, localizing an arbitrary kernel shows the kernel localizes to zero at each prime, hence is zero. This justifies checking flatness locally on schemes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions 24.2.5–24.2.7 — Flat sheaves and flat morphisms
rubrics_metrics.description: A quasicoherent sheaf F on a scheme X is flat at p if F_p is a flat O_{X,p}-module; F is flat if flat at all p. A morphism π:X→Y is flat at p∈X if O_{X,p} is a flat O_{Y,π(p)}-module; π is flat if flat at all p. For a morphism π:X→Y and a quasicoherent sheaf F on X, F is flat over Y at p if F_p is flat as an O_{Y,π(p)}-module.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These definitions reduce to the ring/module case on affines and allow checking flatness on affine covers. They unify module-flatness and morphism-flatness in the geometric setting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flatness preserved under base change and composition
rubrics_metrics.description: If A→B is a ring map and M is a flat B-module, then M ⊗_B A is flat as an A-module (change-of-base preserves flatness). If A is flat over B and M is flat over A, then M is flat over B (composition preserves flatness). For morphisms of schemes, flatness is preserved under base change and composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises 24.2.C, 24.2.D, 24.2.H, and 24.2.I state and invite proving these facts. Use standard tensor / localization / adjunction arguments; base change and composition make flatness a robust geometric property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 24.2.9 — Cohomology commutes with flat base change
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a Cartesian square with π quasicompact and separated and ρ flat, for any quasicoherent sheaf F on X the natural maps ρ^*(Riπ_* F) → Riπ'_* (ρ'^* F) (equivalently ρ^* (Riπ_* F) ≅ Riπ'_* (ρ'^* F)) are isomorphisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the affine (ρ affine) special case (Exercise 18.7.B(a)) and glue via the quasicompact separated hypothesis. The i=0 case only needs quasiseparated. This is an important tool connecting fiber cohomology and higher pushforwards; see subsequent sections for refinements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pullback of closed subschemes by flat morphisms preserves exact sequences of ideal sheaves
rubrics_metrics.description: Under a flat morphism, pullback of ideal sheaves (and the corresponding closed subschemes) preserves exact sequences and powers: (π^* I)^n = π^*(I^n). Pullback of closed subschemes behaves well and is in fact characteristic of flat morphisms (ideal-theoretic criterion, see Theorem 24.4.1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remarks 14.5.8/14.5.10 and exercises 24.2.N–24.2.P illustrate how Cartier divisors, regular embeddings, blowups, and graded algebras behave under flat pullback. Use this to recognize or test flatness in geometric situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization via Tor (section 24.3 and Exercise 23.1.C)
rubrics_metrics.description: M is A-flat if and only if Tor^A_1(M,N) = 0 for all A-modules N (equivalently, Tor^A_i(M,–)=0 for all i>0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives a homological criterion for flatness that is often easier to compute in examples. It is used to derive many consequences and tests for flatness in the chapter (e.g., computing Tor with A/(x) in Exercise 24.3.A).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise 24.3.A — Tor with A/(x) detects torsion
rubrics_metrics.description: If x is not a zerodivisor, then Tor^A_i(M, A/(x)) is M/xM for i=0, (M:x) for i=1, and 0 for i>1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the 2-term resolution 0 → A --×x→ A → A/(x) → 0. This explains the notation Tor (torsion) and shows directly that flatness implies torsion-freeness over integral domains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base-change formula for Tor when extension is flat (Exercise 24.3.B)
rubrics_metrics.description: If B is A-flat, then there is an isomorphism B ⊗_A Tor^A_i(M,N) ≅ Tor^B_i(B⊗_A M, B⊗_A N).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the flatness of B and the FHHF theorem (flat base change for homology of complexes). This is useful to compute Tor after extension of scalars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tensoring exact sequences with a flat module preserves exactness (Exercises 24.3.C–24.3.G)
rubrics_metrics.description: If 0 → N' → N → N'' → 0 is exact and N'' is flat, then tensoring with any module M preserves exactness; similarly, various closure properties: kernels, cokernels, and extensions of flat modules are flat under the usual hypotheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the long exact sequence of Tor and standard homological arguments. Exercises spell out consequences: pulling back exact sequences of sheaves by a flat sheaf remains exact (24.3.D), and finite or infinite exact complexes with all but one term flat imply the remaining term is flat (24.3.F–G).
